items.text: HINT

items.label: text
items.text: Water can act as proton acceptor (base) or proton donor (acid) in reactions on this page. Do not get confused with what is happening here; remember, water is still neutral! We are simply understanding the reactions that occur in terms of proton transfer.

items.text: MORE ACID-BASE REACTIONS

items.label: text
items.text: Acids in solution are acidic because they donate a proton (H⁺) to water to form the hydroxonium ion. If we take a general acid (HA), this is what happens when it is put into water:

items.label: formula
items.text: H A ( a q ) + H _ { 2 } O ( 1 ) \rightarrow H _ { 3 } O ^ { + } ( a q ) + A ^ { - } ( a q )

items.label: text
items.text: HA donates a proton to H2O, which acts as a base. For nitric acid this would be:

items.label: formula
items.text: H N O _ { 3 } ( a q ) + H _ { 2 } O ( l ) \rightarrow H _ { 3 } O ^ { + } ( a q ) + N O _ { 3 } \bar { ( a q ) } \\ a c i d \quad b a s e

items.label: text
items.text: When bases, such as metal oxides (e.g. Na2O), react with water they accept a proton from water, for example:

items.label: text
items.text: The O²- ion accepts a proton from the water. In this reaction the water acts as an acid because it donates a proton.

items.label: text
items.text: When sulfuric acid reacts with copper(ll) oxide (CuO) we have:

items.label: text
items.text: H2SOis an acid, it donates protons to CuO, the base.

items.label: text
items.text: Ammonia is also a base:

items.label: formula
items.text: \ N H _ { 3 } ( a q ) + H _ { 2 } O ( 1 ) \Rightarrow N H _ { 4 } ( a q ) + O H ^ { - } ( a q ) \\ \text {base} \quad \text {acid}

items.label: text
items.text: The ammonia accepts a proton (H⁺) from the water.

items.label: text
items.text: For reactions such as:

items.label: formula
items.text: H C I ( a q ) + N a O H ( a q ) \rightarrow N a C I ( a q ) + H _ { 2 } O ( 1 )

items.label: text
items.text: What actually happens is that the H3O+ ion formed when the acid reacts with water donates a proton to the base, OH-.

items.label: formula
items.text: \begin{smallmatrix} H _ { 3 } O ^ { + } ( a q ) + O H ^ { - } ( a q ) \rightarrow 2 H _ { 2 } O ( 1 ) \\ a c i d & b a s e \end{smallmatrix}

items.label: text
items.text: But for International GCSE purposes, we almost always use the simplified version:

items.label: formula
items.text: H ^ { + } ( a q ) + O H ^ { - } ( a q ) \rightarrow H _ { 2 } O ( 1 )
